extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of political theology and theology (subjects evaluating prophetic and miraculous claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply Hobbes's criteria for judging prophets, visions, and miracles — when to believe, examine, or reject purported supernatural claims, and the sovereign's role in adjudication. Focuses on signs, rarity, natural-cause exclusion, conformity to established doctrine, and public verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine probability of a pretended prophet's calling
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Every Man Ought To Examine The Probability Of A Pretended Prophets Calling' — use Reason and Judgement to discern between natural and supernatural gifts, and be circumspect before yielding obedience to one who pretends to be a Prophet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason and judgement must distinguish naturall from supernaturall Gifts and Visions (dreams), because extraordinary gifts are rare and often proceed by natural mediation; prophets who claim to govern or promise great felicity should be suspected of ambition and imposture and therefore tried by the marks God prescribed (e.g., Deut.13; 1 John 4). Examples: many more false than true prophets (Ahab's 400 false prophets vs. one Micaiah); Jeremiah's rebuke of lying prophets. If not authorised by the civil commonwealth, individuals must examine claims before obeying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to the sovereign prophet's doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophet must teach doctrine conformable to that which the sovereign Prophet (or established religious head) has taught; do not accept teachers who teach another religion or doctrine contrary to the lawful Head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes repeatedly cites Moses's rule: 'take not any for Prophets, that teach any other Religion, then that which Gods Lieutenant ... hath established.' In the New Testament the decisive mark is confession that 'Jesus Christ is come in the flesh' (1 John 4): 'Every Spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, is of God.' If a pretended prophet's doctrine contradicts the sovereign-established public doctrine, he is to be rejected. This is the primary test in community contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictions must come to pass (test by fulfilled prophecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: One test of a prophet is that his predictions are seen to come to pass; if prophetic predictions fail, the speaker is a false prophet (per Deut.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes endorses Moses's rule that prophecy should be examined by whether its words come to pass. Failure of foretold events is grounds for rejecting the prophet: 'Moses therefore ... and the other the miraculous power of foretelling what God would bring to passe.' Use observation and verification of predicted events as a test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles must be rare and lack any natural cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A Miracle is a work that causeth Admiration: it must be both strange (rare) and such that we cannot imagine any natural cause for it — otherwise it is not a miracle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes defines wonder as arising from strangeness or from lack of imaginable natural cause. Examples: a speaking horse would be a miracle; the first rainbow was a miracle because it was the first and strange. When a natural cause is known or a similar event is frequent, we cease to call it a miracle. Therefore, to qualify, an event must be both unusual and not explainable by ordinary natural or human means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles are wrought to procure credit to God's messengers
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper end of miracles is to procure credit to God's Messengers, Ministers, and Prophets so that men may know they are sent by God; otherwise admirable works are not properly called miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that many admirable acts (creation, the deluge) are not termed 'miracles' because they were not done to authenticate a messenger. Miracles are ordinarily wrought 'for the making manifest to his elect, the mission of an extraordinary Minister for their salvation.' Thus one should ask whether the wondrous event was intended to validate a messenger's mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles must be immediate works of God (not by created spirits or incantation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true miracle must be the immediate hand of God (not an effect of Devils, Angels acting independently, or incantations); if wrought by other created powers or by mediation, it is not a true miracle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes reasons that if an effect comes from incantation, human art, or power given to a created spirit, then it is not the immediate work of God and thus not strictly a miracle. Texts that seem to attribute wonders to magicians (e.g., Egyptian magicians imitating Moses) must be reinterpreted as imposture or natural means. This is an exclusionary criterion: only divine immediacy counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept miracles on hearsay — require direct observation and public verification
rubrics_metrics.description: One must both see the miracle done and use all means to consider whether it really was done; if you only hear of a miracle, consult the lawful Head of the Church/sovereign to determine credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes advises that claims of miracles reported secondhand require consultation with the lawful head (the public lieutenant of God) before public assent: 'If we see not, but onely hear tell of a Miracle, we are to consult the Lawful Church.' Private belief in one's heart is free, but public confession or obedience must submit to public judgment. Example: alleged transmutation of bread should be investigated and not believed from report alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private judgement vs public (sovereign) judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: In doubtful cases of miraculous claims, private men may hold belief privately but must submit public confession and obedience to the judgement of the sovereign (God's Lieutenant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes private inward belief (which remains free) from outward obedience and public faith. Because society depends on civil peace, the public reason of the sovereign is the arbiter of contested supernatural claims. Thus the community's sovereign becomes the judge of which miracles/prophets are authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent miracles vary with knowledge — beware deception from ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That Which Seemeth A Miracle To One Man, May Seem Otherwise To Another' — whether an event appears miraculous depends on the observer's knowledge and experience; ignorance and superstition make people apt to be deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes gives examples: eclipses mistaken for supernatural events by the ignorant; ventriloquism and jugglery deceiving the unwary; conspiracies and staged cures. Evaluate claims with regard to the observers' expertise; consult those with natural knowledge before concluding the supernatural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many alleged miracles are impostures (magick, enchantment, confederacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent miraculous effects produced by magicians, enchantments, or confederacies are often natural impostures, tricks, or deceptions rather than true divine miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes explains how conjuring, confederacy, and exploitation of ignorance can create convincing 'wonders' (e.g., staged lame persons healed by accomplices). Words alone affect only those who understand them; so-called enchantments often merely deceive spectators. Treat reports of magic with scepticism and seek natural explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles are meant chiefly to beget belief in the elect, not to convert all
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of miracles is to beget or confirm belief (often only in the elect); miracles do not necessarily persuade all men or produce universal conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes that miracles served to add 'to the Church' those whom God had elected, not to convert hardened or reprobate hearts (e.g., Pharaoh hardened despite the plagues). Thus the presence or absence of universal belief does not by itself invalidate a miracle's divine origin, but one must recognize the limited intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate prophecy is derivative of the sovereign prophet's Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy by subordinate or perpetually-called prophets was subordinate to the sovereign prophet (e.g., Moses): their spirit or gift was given from the sovereign, and they prophesied as the sovereign would have them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes cites Numbers 11 where God 'took of the Spirit that was upon [Moses], and gave it to the seventy Elders,' showing their prophecy was 'subservient, and subordinate to the Prophecying of Moses.' Thus subordinate prophetic authority is legitimate only insofar as it derives from and concurs with the sovereign's authority; otherwise it ought not to be accepted.
